summary: Defines the Matroska audiovisual container format, including its structural elements, terminology, and vocabulary. It also updates RFC 8794 to allow use of a previously reserved Extensible Binary Meta Language (EBML) Element ID.

eli5.summary: A video file is like a lunchbox with compartments for picture, sound, and subtitles. Matroska is a well-known design for such a lunchbox.

questions: what is the difference between mkv and ebml
subtitle: The open container format that packs video, audio, subtitles, chapters and tags into one file, built on EBML.

tldr.problem: A movie needs many streams (video, several audio tracks, subtitles) plus chapters, tags and attachments, and they have to live together in one file that can be seeked, streamed and extended without breaking old players.
tldr.mechanism: Matroska is a document type of EBML, a binary derivative of XML. A Segment holds top-level elements such as Info, Tracks, Clusters of Blocks, Cues, Chapters, Attachments and Tags, and version fields tell readers what to expect.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9559 documents Matroska versions 1 to 4 as a Proposed Standard, creates IANA registries for its element IDs and value lists, and updates RFC 8794 so that the one-octet EBML ID 0x80 is legal.

facts.label: Cluster size advice
facts.value: No more than five seconds or five megabytes

today: RFC 9559 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 8794 so that the one-octet EBML ID 0x80 is legal, and it states that Matroska version 4 is the current version.

sections.title: What Matroska Is and Is Not
sections.content:
Matroska is an audiovisual data container format. It was derived from a project called MCF but diverges from it significantly because it is based on EBML (Extensible Binary Meta Language, defined in RFC 8794), a binary derivative of XML. EBML gives the format room to grow without breaking parsers that read earlier versions.

The RFC is careful about what a container is. It is not a video or audio compression format (a codec). It is an envelope in which there can be many audio, video and subtitle streams, so a complete movie or CD can be stored in a single file.

The design goals listed are fast seeking, chapter entries, full metadata (tags) support, selectable subtitle, audio and video streams, modular expandability, error resilience, streaming over the Internet and local networks (HTTP, FTP, SMB and others), and menus like those of a DVD.

The document covers Matroska versions 1, 2, 3 and 4. Version 4 is the current one. Versions 1 to 3 are no longer maintained and no new elements are expected in files with those version numbers. It defines terms for its roles: Matroska Reader (a parser), Matroska Player (a reader whose main purpose is playback) and Matroska Writer (a creator of documents).
sections.eli5: Matroska is the box, not the movie. The box has room for pictures, sounds, subtitles and labels, and it does not care how each one was squeezed down to fit.

sections.title: EBML Rules and Versioning
sections.content:
Matroska is a Document Type of EBML. It adds a few constraints: the docType of the EBML Header MUST be matroska, EBMLMaxIDLength MUST be 4, and EBMLMaxSizeLength MUST be between 1 and 8. The Root Element and all Top-Level Elements MUST use 4 octets for their Element ID. Writers MUST NOT use EBML Empty Elements when the element has a default value that is not 0 for integers and dates, or 0x0p+0 for floats, because legacy parsers wrongly assumed those values.

This RFC also updates RFC 8794. Because of an oversight, RFC 8794 reserved the one-octet EBML ID 0x80, which deployed Matroska implementations already use. The fix makes 0x80 a legal ID, so one-octet IDs run from 0x80 to 0xFE (127 valid IDs instead of 126) and only 0xFF stays reserved.

Matroska is built on the idea that a reader does not need to support 100 percent of the specification to play a file. The EBML Header carries DocTypeVersion, which MUST be equal to or greater than the highest Matroska version of any element in the file, and DocTypeReadVersion, the minimum version a reader needs to play it back, possibly with fewer features. A reader that supports version V MUST NOT refuse a file whose read version is V or lower, and it MUST skip unknown elements that fit inside their parent.
sections.eli5: Every file carries a note saying how new its newest feature is and how new a player has to be to play it. A player that is a bit old can still play the file and just ignore the fancy extras it does not understand.

sections.title: File Layout and Top-Level Elements
sections.content:
A Matroska file is at least one EBML Document: an EBML Header followed by the Root Element, called Segment. A file can also be an EBML Stream of several such documents back to back. The Segment holds eight Top-Level Elements:

  • SeekHead: an index of where the other Top-Level Elements are. Its use is RECOMMENDED, because without it a parser may have to search the whole file.
  • Info: identifies the Segment (title, a randomly generated UID, the UIDs of linked Segments, TimestampScale, Duration).
  • Tracks: the technical details of each track, such as its number, UID, language, type and codec, and for video the resolution or for audio the sampling frequency.
  • Chapters: predefined points to jump to in video or audio.
  • Cluster: the actual content, such as video frames.
  • Cues: a temporal index used for seeking.
  • Attachments: files such as pictures and fonts.
  • Tags: metadata about the Segment and its tracks, chapters and attachments.

Only Info is REQUIRED. To be playable, a file MUST also contain at least one Tracks and one Cluster element, and the first Info and Tracks either come before the first Cluster or are both referenced by a SeekHead placed before it.

Section 5 of the RFC is an EBML Schema that defines every element with its ID, type, path, allowed occurrences and rules. The Segment itself has ID 0x18538067. This explainer does not reproduce that schema, which is the bulk of the document.
sections.eli5: Inside the lunchbox there is a table of contents, a name tag, a list of what is packed, the food itself in small trays, and an index and notes at the back. Only the name tag is truly required.

sections.title: Clusters, Blocks and Lacing
sections.content:
Media data lives in Clusters. Each Cluster MUST contain exactly one Timestamp, which SHOULD be its first child (or second if the Cluster starts with a CRC-32). The RFC RECOMMENDS that a Cluster hold no more than five seconds or five megabytes of content. Frames go into a Block inside a BlockGroup, or into a SimpleBlock placed directly in the Cluster. SimpleBlock is usually preferred unless extra BlockGroup elements are needed, and a reader MUST support both.

A block starts with a variable-length header: the track number as an EBML variable-size integer (up to 8 octets, shortest form SHOULD be used), a 16-bit signed timestamp relative to the Cluster, and a flags octet. The flags include an Invisible bit (decode but do not display) and two LACING bits. A SimpleBlock adds a Keyframe flag and a Discardable flag.

Lacing packs several small frames into one block to save space. It MUST NOT be used for a single frame. There are three kinds:

  • Xiph lacing (inspired by Ogg): each size is written as a run of 0xFF octets plus a final remainder, so 500 is coded 255;245. RECOMMENDED only for small frames.
  • EBML lacing: the first size is an EBML variable-size integer and later sizes are signed differences from the previous frame size.
  • Fixed-size lacing: only the frame count is stored, and every frame MUST have the same size.

In all three, the size of the last frame is deduced from what remains in the block. Laced frames MUST be contiguous with no gap between them, so lacing suits audio and SHOULD NOT be used for subtitles.

For random access, frames that depend on others MUST be marked: a SimpleBlock has its keyframe flag clear, or the BlockGroup contains one or more ReferenceBlock elements. Frames that depend on nothing MUST set the keyframe flag, or sit in a BlockGroup with no ReferenceBlock.
sections.eli5: Frames are packed in trays called blocks. If the pieces are tiny, you can put several into one tray and write down their sizes so nobody has to guess where one ends and the next begins.

sections.title: How Timestamps Work
sections.content:
Every time value in Matroska is a multiple of a tick. There are three kinds. Matroska Ticks are plain nanoseconds, used by elements such as DefaultDuration and ChapterTimeStart. Segment Ticks are scaled by the Segment's TimestampScale (default 1000000, so one tick is one millisecond), used by Cluster\Timestamp, Duration and CueTime. Track Ticks also apply the track's TrackTimestampScale, which is usually omitted and treated as 1.0. Many readers ignore a value other than 1.0, so using one might not work.

A block's own timestamp is a signed 16-bit offset (from -32768 to +32767 Track Ticks) added to the Cluster Timestamp. For example, if the Cluster Timestamp is 10 seconds and a Block plays at 12 seconds, the Block stores 2 seconds. The result SHOULD NOT be negative, and if a CodecDelay is set it MUST be subtracted. A frame that ends up with a negative timestamp MUST be decoded but not played.

The RFC notes that timestamps were historically, and mistakenly, called timecodes, which is why older names such as TimecodeScale exist.
sections.eli5: Each tray has a clock that says how long after the start of its shelf to play. You add the shelf time and the tray offset to get the exact moment.

sections.title: Linked Segments, Chapters and Cues
sections.content:
Several Segments can be joined into one presentation, called a Linked Segment. All of them MUST have a SegmentUUID. With Hard Linking (also called splitting), Segments point to each other with PrevUUID and NextUUID, MUST share the same Tracks list and TimestampScale, and their timestamps MUST follow on from the previous Segment. If the two links disagree, NextUUID takes precedence.

Medium Linking uses Ordered Chapters and the ChapterSegmentUUID element. A chapter can play a time range of another Segment (Linked-Duration, where ChapterTimeEnd MUST be set) or a whole edition of it (Linked-Edition).

Chapters are grouped into Editions. In Simple Chapters only the start time is a marker. If EditionFlagOrdered is set, a player MUST play the chapters in their stored order from start to end time, which lets one file hold several edits of a film without duplicating content. Chapters can be nested, and the first Edition with EditionFlagDefault true is the default (or the first Edition if none is flagged).

Cues index Clusters for seeking. Each CuePoint MUST give a time, a track and a Segment Position. Unless the file is a live stream it SHOULD contain Cues, each video keyframe SHOULD be referenced, and audio references SHOULD be at most once every 500 milliseconds.
sections.eli5: A long show can be split over several lunchboxes that say which box comes next. Chapters are bookmarks, and an ordered list of bookmarks can even skip parts or pull in a clip from a different box.

sections.title: Track Flags and Default Track Selection
sections.content:
Tracks carry flags that help a player choose what to play. The Default flag marks a track as eligible for automatic selection for its language, as opposed to specialized services. The Forced flag says a subtitle track SHOULD be shown even when user preferences would show none, for example to translate on-screen text. Other flags mark Hearing-Impaired, Visual-Impaired, Descriptions, Original-language and Commentary tracks. A player MAY override the Default flag, including to follow accessibility preferences.

Section 19 walks through example track sets. A player first considers language, then flags like Original and Visual-Impaired, then can use channel layout (stereo for headphones, surround for a surround system). If several tracks still look equally good, it SHOULD pick the first.

Video presentation is also controlled by the file. The PixelCrop elements say how many rows or columns SHOULD be cropped before display; the RFC's example is a 1440x1080 picture inside a padded 1920x1080 frame, with 240 columns cropped on each side. Rotation is given by ProjectionPoseRoll, where 90 means a 90-degree counter-clockwise presentation.
sections.eli5: The file puts little stickers on each track, like English, Spanish, extra-loud, or director talking. A player reads the stickers and your settings and picks the track that suits you.

sections.title: Element Ordering, Streaming and Layouts
sections.content:
EBML requires no particular order except for the EBML Header and CRC-32, but Matroska adds ordering rules for better playback and editing. A CRC-32 element, if used, MUST be first in its parent, and all Top-Level Elements SHOULD include one (the Segment SHOULD NOT). The first SeekHead MUST be the first non-CRC-32 child of the Segment, and the SeekHeads together MUST reference all other Top-Level Elements. When new top-level elements are added to an existing file, the SeekHead MUST be updated, and Void elements can be used as padding to avoid moving large amounts of data.

The RFC gives an optimum layout for a muxer: SeekHead, Info, Tracks, Chapters, Attachments, Tags, Clusters, then Cues. After editing tags, the old Tags are voided and the new ones are written at the end. Putting Cues at the front helps seeking but is rarely used because the space is hard to reserve.

For file access (local files, HTTP, CIFS), Matroska does not need its index loaded before playing, so playback can start quickly. For livestreaming, the Segment size field has all bits set to 1 because the end is unknown, or Segments of known size are concatenated, which allows a codec or resolution change. In a live stream, SeekHead, Cues, Chapters and Attachments MUST NOT be used when Segments are continuous. Matroska is not meant to be used over RTP, which already has its own timing and channel mechanisms.
sections.eli5: The best way to pack the box is to put the table of contents and name tags at the front, the food in the middle, and the index at the back. For a live show, you skip the index because nobody knows when it ends.

sections.title: Security and Encryption
sections.content:
Matroska inherits the security considerations of EBML. The RFC lists attacks on a Reader: arbitrary and potentially executable data stored in an Attachments element (readers that use attachments SHOULD check that the data meets expectations or not use it), an attachment with an inaccurate media type, damaged encryption or compression fields that produce bogus data for the decoder, and Chapter Codecs running unwanted commands on the host. Readers need to be robust against malicious payloads, including the denial of service issues in RFC 4732, and Writers must not misbehave on malicious stream data. Implementers must also consider the security of the codecs whose streams are carried inside.

Error handling is left to implementations. For instance, with an invalid checksum on Tracks, some readers try to read anyway, some reject the file, and most do not check it.

On encryption, the specification provides no interoperable solution for confidentiality, integrity, authenticity or authorization. The ContentEncryption fields exist only so implementers can build their own proprietary schemes or further standards, and key management is out of scope. A Writer MUST NOT use insecure cryptographic algorithms to create new archives or streams, though a Reader MAY support them to read old ones.
sections.eli5: A box can hold surprises, so a player should not blindly trust what it finds inside, like a strange note telling it to run a program. The lock on the box is left for each maker to design.

sections.title: IANA Registries and Media Types
sections.content:
The RFC asks IANA to create a set of registries so that Matroska can keep growing. The main one is the Matroska Element IDs registry. One-octet IDs (0x80 to 0xFE) are allocated by the 'RFC Required' policy, two-octet IDs (0x407F to 0x7FFE) by 'Specification Required', and three- and four-octet IDs by 'First Come First Served'. Given the scarcity of one-octet IDs, they should be used sparingly. Further registries cover compression and encryption algorithms, AES cipher modes, content encoding scopes and types, stereo and alpha modes, display units, chroma siting, color ranges, tag target types, chapter codec IDs, projection types, track types and track plane types.

It also registers three media types: video/matroska for files with video tracks, audio/matroska for audio with no video, and video/matroska-3d for files containing a stereoscopic video track. The older x-matroska names are listed as deprecated aliases.

Appendix A lists historic deprecated elements that existed in earlier versions and should no longer be used in new files.
sections.eli5: There is a public sign-up book where new labels for the box must be written down, so two people never pick the same label for different things.

fields.desc: EBML VINT-coded track number; can be 8 to 56 bits.

fields.desc: Signed timestamp in Track Ticks, relative to the Cluster.

fields.desc: Invisible: decode the frame but do not display it.

cells: Runs of 255 plus remainder, as in Ogg
Not stored; all frames the same size

data.title: Block timestamp in nanoseconds
data.code:
Segment Ticks:
  timestamp in nanosecond = element value * TimestampScale

Block or SimpleBlock:
  ( Cluster\Timestamp + ( block timestamp * TrackTimestampScale ) ) *
  TimestampScale

With CodecDelay set:
  ( ( Cluster\Timestamp + ( block timestamp * TrackTimestampScale ) ) *
    TimestampScale ) - CodecDelay
